results.content:
Title: Sentiment Analysis with Transformers
We compared the performance of traditional architectures such as LSTM with the state-of-the-art transformer-based models like BERT and BART, to determine the most effective approach for text-based sentiment analysis. The methodology was pretty straight forward - pre-process the data, train the models on the data, and then evaluate each of them. The batch sizes for the LSTM, BERT, and BART models were 256, 64, and 32. Tokenization was performed differently for the transformer-based models and LSTM. Unlike the original Transformer architecture which contains both Encoder and Decoder parts, BERT model only uses Encoder part, which consists of It processes input text in a fully bidirectional manner, meaning it considers both the left and right context of each token. epochs =  3  learning_rate =  2e-5  total_steps =  len(train_dataset)  *  epochs optimizer =  AdamW(bert_model. step()   avg_loss =  total_loss /  len(train_dataset)   accuracy =  accuracy_score(true_labels,  predictions)   return  avg_loss,  accuracy  def  evaluate(model):   model. numpy())   avg_loss =  total_loss /  len(val_dataset)   accuracy =  accuracy_score(true_labels,  predictions)   return  avg_loss,  accuracy  def  test_evaluate(model):   model. append(train_acc)   val_loss,  val_acc =  evaluate(bert_model)   print(f"Eval Loss: {val_loss:.4f} ")   print(f"Eval Accuracy: {val_acc:.4f} ")   val_loss_history. The model training and evaluation was done using the custom loop which we used for BERT:. The LSTM model was trained for 4 epochs, the transformer-based models were trained for 3 epochs each. All models were evaluated on the same metrics, which included Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-Score, and ROC-AUC Score and we also generated Classification Report using Scikit-Learn which included a class-wise breakdown of the metrics. The Bi-LSTM model performed robustly as a baseline for the sentiment analysis task, achieving a weighted precision, recall, and F1-score of 0.8271, along with a ROC-AUC of 0.827. The BERT model demonstrated strong performance on the sentiment analysis task, achieving an overall accuracy of 85.02%, with weighted precision, recall, and F1-score all around 0.85, and a ROC-AUC of 0.85, indicating excellent class separation ability. BART model demonstrates strong performance, as evidenced by the training and validation metrics. This project explored sentiment analysis using deep learning models, starting with a Bi-LSTM as a baseline and progressing to transformer-based architectures, BERT and BART. The Bi-LSTM model delivered solid baseline performance, while BERT significantly improved accuracy and contextual understanding.

results.title: How do you build a text classifier?
results.content: * How do you build a text classifier? # How do you build a text classifier? Building a text classifier involves three main phases: data preparation, model selection/training, and evaluation/deployment. The process starts with collecting and preprocessing text data, then selecting an appropriate algorithm, and finally testing and operationalizing the model. Each step requires careful consideration of the problem’s specifics, such as the type of text data and the desired classification accuracy. Start by gathering a labeled dataset relevant to your classification task—for example, product reviews labeled as “positive” or “negative.” Clean the text by removing noise like special characters, HTML tags, or irrelevant punctuation. Use tokenization (splitting text into words or subwords) and normalization (lowercasing, stemming) to standardize the input. Traditional methods like TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) weight words based on their importance in a document, while modern approaches like word embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe) or transformer-based embeddings (BERT) capture semantic meaning. For instance, using scikit-learn’s `TfidfVectorizer` can transform raw text into a matrix of TF-IDF scores, which serves as input for machine learning models. Next, **model selection and training** depend on the problem’s complexity and data size. For more nuanced tasks—like sentiment analysis with context-dependent language—deep learning models like RNNs (LSTMs) or transformer architectures (BERT, DistilBERT) are better suited. Use frameworks like TensorFlow or PyTorch for neural networks, or scikit-learn for classical models. For example, fine-tuning a pre-trained BERT model using Hugging Face’s `transformers` library can achieve high accuracy with limited labeled data by leveraging transfer learning. Finally, **evaluation and deployment** ensure the model performs reliably. Measure performance using metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, or F1-score, depending on class balance and business needs. Once validated, deploy the model as an API (using Flask or FastAPI) or integrate it into applications via cloud services like AWS SageMaker. Monitor the model’s performance over time and retrain it periodically with new data to maintain accuracy. Tools like MLflow or Kubeflow streamline deployment and monitoring workflows, ensuring scalability and maintainability. results.title: Text Classification for Sentiment Analysis – Precision and Recall | StreamHacker
results.content: This time, instead of measuring accuracy, we’ll collect reference values and observed values for each label (pos or neg), then use those sets to calculate the precision, recall, and F-measure of the naive bayes classifier. [sourcecode language="python"] import collections import nltk.metrics from nltk.classify import NaiveBayesClassifier from nltk.corpus import movie_reviews def word_feats(words): return dict([(word, True) for word in words]) negids = movie_reviews.fileids('neg') posids = movie_reviews.fileids('pos') negfeats = [(word_feats(movie_reviews.words(fileids=[f])), 'neg') for f in negids] posfeats = [(word_feats(movie_reviews.words(fileids=[f])), 'pos') for f in posids] negcutoff = len(negfeats)*3/4 poscutoff = len(posfeats)*3/4 trainfeats = negfeats[:negcutoff] + posfeats[:poscutoff] testfeats = negfeats[negcutoff:] + posfeats[poscutoff:] print 'train on %d instances, test on %d instances' % (len(trainfeats), len(testfeats)) classifier = NaiveBayesClassifier.train(trainfeats) refsets = collections.defaultdict(set) testsets = collections.defaultdict(set) for i, (feats, label) in enumerate(testfeats): refsets[label].add(i) observed = classifier.classify(feats) testsets[observed].add(i) print 'pos precision:', nltk.metrics.precision(refsets['pos'], testsets['pos']) print 'pos recall:', nltk.metrics.recall(refsets['pos'], testsets['pos']) print 'pos F-measure:', nltk.metrics.f_measure(refsets['pos'], testsets['pos']) print 'neg precision:', nltk.metrics.precision(refsets['neg'], testsets['neg']) print 'neg recall:', nltk.metrics.recall(refsets['neg'], testsets['neg']) print 'neg F-measure:', nltk.metrics.f_measure(refsets['neg'], testsets['neg']) [/sourcecode].

results.title: Precision, Recall, AUC: The Ultimate Guide to Classification Metrics
results.content: # Precision, Recall, AUC: The Ultimate Guide to Classification Metrics. This blog covers all about model evaluation metrics for classification problems. These models are designed to predict a category for a given input. 1. Single-Class Classification A classifier that predicts only one class for each input is called a single-class classifier. 2. Multi-Class Classification A classifier that predicts multiple classes for an input is called a multi-class classifier. ## Model Evaluation Metrics for Classifiers. Model evaluation metrics help us understand the prediction accuracy of a model for each class. The prediction class for which we are calculating matrics is called positive (wanted prediction) class and remaining classes will be negative (Unwanted Prediction). True refers to accurate prediction by model and False refers to inaccurate prediction by model. Accuracy is measure of rate of correct predcitions out of all inputs to model, accuracy tells you how many predictions are correct out of you provided to model. But what if you want to know accuracy for perticular class from prediction, and this curiosity brings new matrics called precision. Model accuracy for a particular class is nothing but the precision for that class. Precision indicates how well our model is performing for a specific class. Prediction, also called accuracy of positive predictions, is measured using precision, which is calculated for each class in the dataset. Recall is responsible to calculate True Positive rate of our model and also called sesitivity matrics. Confusion matrix is a way of representing model predictions for each class with two axis true axis and predicted axis. For example, if the actual class is 1, but the model predicts it as class 0, that would be a misclassification. This blog comprehensively explores model evaluation metrics for classification problems in machine learning. The core focus lies in explaining essential evaluation metrics that help assess and improve the performance of classification models. 2. Precision: Indicates the accuracy of positive predictions, focusing on a specific class. 5. Confusion Matrix: Visualizes model predictions for all classes, highlighting both correct and incorrect classifications. 6. ROC AUC Curve: Evaluates the model's performance across all possible thresholds, providing a holistic view of True Positive Rate (TPR) vs.
